content: When breastfeeding ends, antiretroviral therapy (ART) should be discontinued in cases where replacement feeding is used after delivery. Antiretroviral (ARV) drugs are primarily administered to pregnant and breastfeeding women with HIV to protect the mother’s health and prevent HIV transmission to the child. Additionally, these drugs may reduce the risk of sexual transmission of HIV. The 2010 World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines for the prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) recommended lifelong ART for women eligible for treatment based on a CD4 count of ≤350 cells/mm³ or the presence of WHO clinical stage 3 or 4 disease. For women not eligible for treatment, two prophylaxis regimens were suggested: “Option A,” which involved zidovudine (AZT) during pregnancy and a combination of single-dose nevirapine (NVP), AZT, and lamivudine (3TC) during delivery and postpartum; and “Option B,” which involved triple ARV therapy during pregnancy and breastfeeding. Prophylaxis was recommended to begin as early as 14 weeks of gestation, with additional ARV coverage for the infant for 4–6 weeks postpartum, regardless of breastfeeding status. Countries were advised to adopt a national approach to PMTCT based on operational considerations. In 2011, Malawi introduced a new approach called “Option B+,” which provided lifelong ART to all pregnant and breastfeeding women with HIV, regardless of CD4 count or clinical stage. WHO highlighted the operational advantages of this strategy in a 2012 update. The 2013 WHO guidelines recommended a simplified triple-drug ART regimen for all pregnant and breastfeeding women with HIV during the period of risk for mother-to-child transmission and, in some cases, lifelong ART. Option A was no longer recommended due to its complexity, which hindered PMTCT scale-up in many countries. Lifelong ART for all pregnant and breastfeeding women offers several benefits, including ease of implementation, harmonization with adult ART guidelines, increased ART coverage, prevention of vertical transmission, improved maternal health, and reduced sexual transmission of HIV. Community acceptance of this approach has also been strong. The recommendation to provide lifelong ART to all pregnant and breastfeeding women with HIV is conditional, depending on the epidemic setting and country program. However, in settings with concentrated epidemics, high CD4 testing access, and low fertility rates, ART may be discontinued in women not eligible for treatment after the risk of mother-to-child transmission has ended. Implementation research is also needed to address knowledge gaps related to lifelong ART. Transitioning from the 2010 to the 2013 guidelines requires careful planning, with countries currently using Option A encouraged to adopt lifelong ART for all pregnant and breastfeeding women. The 2013 guidelines also emphasized the importance of providing ART to all children under five years of age with HIV, regardless of clinical stage or CD4 count, due to their high risk of poor outcomes. Infants diagnosed within the first year of life should receive immediate ART. For children aged 1–5 years, ART initiation is recommended, with priority given to those with advanced disease or low CD4 counts. For children aged five years and older, ART should be initiated if the CD4 count is ≤500 cells/mm³, with priority for those with CD4 counts ≤350 cells/mm³ or advanced disease. Research is needed to optimize adherence to ART during breastfeeding and to evaluate the long-term health outcomes of children exposed to ARVs through breast milk.
